title: Partner Enablement: Redwood Standard Demo v1 + joint-call runbook
summary: Partner enablement session for VectorBridge Partners on Redwood’s Standard Demo v1. Redwood team walked through demo tenant purpose, access controls, “known-good” scenario flow, and how to run a joint customer call (driver vs narrator roles). Covered how to position Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, what proof points are safe to claim live, and how to handle common security questions (logging/retention, encryption, audit logs, data residency). Reviewed contingency plans for live-demo instability (fallback scenario, canned outputs, dashboard screenshots).
topics: Demo tenant overview and what it is/isn’t
Access patterns (RBAC, time-bound creds, SSO expectations)
Standard Demo v1 scenario order + variants (2-min mini demo vs full)
How to run a joint call (roles, handoffs, Q&A ownership)
Security FAQ highlights (retention, encryption, audit logs, residency)
Failure modes and backup plan (plan B steps)
Partner-specific logistics: regions, who can request tenant access, escalation path
questions: Can partners get direct access to the Redwood demo tenant, or must Redwood drive every live click?
What’s the approved way to talk about data retention and whether prompts are used for training?
If a customer asks for EU-only routing during the demo, what do we show today vs what do we promise?
Do we show pricing numbers in the deck or keep it at ranges?
What is the escalation path if the tenant is slow 30 minutes before a joint call?
action_items: Renee Sullivan (Redwood) - Share partner-friendly demo quickstart (curl + SDK snippets) and the ‘2-minute hosted mini-demo’ variant script - Due 2025-01-24
Soojin Lee (Redwood) - Send latest Standard Demo v1 deck link + speaker notes, with highlighted ‘safe claims’ sections - Due 2025-01-24
Rafael Mendes (Redwood) - Provide demo incident escalation path (business-hours oncall, Slack channel, what info to capture) - Due 2025-01-24
Elena Petrova (VectorBridge) - Confirm which partner SEs need demo-tenant access and submit list for RBAC - Due 2025-01-27
James Wu (VectorBridge) - Draft a joint-call agenda template (who speaks when, discovery questions) and share with Redwood for review - Due 2025-01-29
next_steps: VectorBridge to nominate 2–3 partner SEs for enablement + access.
Redwood to send the latest deck, talk track, security FAQ, and demo reset checklist links.
Schedule a 30-minute dry run with VectorBridge as ‘customer persona’ (security-heavy).
Agree on joint-call division of labor (partner opens, Redwood drives console, partner handles procurement questions unless technical).
transcript:
MEETING HEADER
Title: Partner Enablement: Redwood Standard Demo v1 + joint-call runbook
Recorded: 2025-01-23 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 min
Attendees (Redwood): Markus Klein, Soojin Lee, Renee Sullivan, Rafael Mendes
Attendees (VectorBridge Partners): Elena Petrova, James Wu, Amina Hassan, Tom Becker

Auto-Summary (Fireflies)
- Goal: enable VectorBridge to co-sell Redwood using the Standard Demo tenant and talk track.
- Outcome: clarified access model, joint-call roles, what to show live, and escalation path.

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool, alright. Folks can hear me okay?
[00:03] Elena Petrova: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:04] James Wu: Yeah, good.
[00:06] Markus Klein: Great. So this is partner enablement for the Standard Demo v1. We’ll do a quick overview of the demo tenant, like what it is and what it is not, then we’ll talk through how we run a joint call. Soojin will cover the narrative and “safe claims,” and then Rafael will cover the, uh, “if stuff goes sideways” playbook.
[00:25] Soojin Lee: And I’ll also flag which slides we tend to skip for time depending on persona.

[00:31] Amina Hassan: Just to level set, our team has two calls next week with EU customers. We want to make sure we don’t overpromise on residency.
[00:39] Markus Klein: Yep, perfect. We’ll hit that.

[00:42] Markus Klein: First: demo tenant. Think of it as a stable sandbox that’s configured to be repeatable. It has pinned model versions, pinned routing policies, quotas set so you don’t get weird 429s mid-call, and dashboards pre-built. It is not a customer trial environment and it’s not meant for running customer data through.
[01:03] Tom Becker: So it’s like… a shared environment for go-to-market?
[01:06] Markus Klein: Exactly. It’s internal-facing + partner-facing, controlled. It’s designed so you can reset it quickly.

[01:13] Renee Sullivan: And to be clear, we also have scripts. Like curl scripts, and small SDK snippets. So the “demo” doesn’t depend on someone typing perfectly under pressure.
[01:23] Elena Petrova: Love that.

[01:25] Markus Klein: On access. There are basically two patterns. Pattern A: Redwood drives everything live. Partner narrates and handles discovery and stakeholder management. Pattern B: partner has limited RBAC access to the tenant to run the API calls, but Redwood still tends to drive the Console portions because that’s where it’s easiest to mis-click.
[01:46] James Wu: When you say limited RBAC, what exactly do we get? Like can we edit routes?
[01:50] Markus Klein: Generally no. We don’t want partners editing routes on the fly. We can set you up with “Demo Runner” role: you can view dashboards, execute requests via API keys, view routes, but not change routing policy or model pinning. It’s basically read-only plus usage.
[02:08] Rafael Mendes: And if there’s a need to show “rollout config,” we usually show it as view-only in Console and talk about how it’s configured. If we need to actually change it live, that’s a Redwood-led moment.

[02:22] Elena Petrova: How are keys distributed? Email? Vault?
[02:26] Renee Sullivan: We do time-bound keys. Typically we provision per partner SE, it’s tied to SSO email, and we rotate. For joint calls we’ll send the key via 1Password share or our secure note system, not plain email.
[02:40] Tom Becker: And revocation is quick?
[02:42] Rafael Mendes: Yeah, immediate. It’s a single key per persona, and we can kill it.

[02:47] Markus Klein: Okay, Soojin, do you want to jump into flow?
[02:50] Soojin Lee: Yep. So the Standard Demo v1 is designed to show four differentiators without getting cute: performance controls, reliability/fallback, deployment flexibility, and observability.
[03:02] Soojin Lee: Typical flow is:
1) 2–3 minute Hosted API quick win: streaming chat with a deterministic prompt set.
2) Then we show cost/latency breakdown in Console. Not exact dollars unless approved, but “token cost per request,” latency percentiles.
3) Then we show routing and fallback: primary model + fallback variant if errors or if capacity is constrained.
4) If the persona is security/platform, we pivot to Dedicated/Private slides: VPC/private control plane narrative, audit logs, KMS, SSO/RBAC.

[03:34] Amina Hassan: When you say deterministic prompt set, do you mean the output is fixed?
[03:39] Renee Sullivan: Not fully fixed. We do a couple things: low temperature, a constrained task, and we keep an “expected output” snippet so you can sanity check quickly. And if it varies, the talk track has a line like, “content can vary, what we’re measuring is latency/cost/controls.”
[03:57] Soojin Lee: Exactly. Also we avoid anything too open-ended like “write a poem.”

[04:05] James Wu: What’s the best story if a customer is like “we have an internal model” or “we’re using Bedrock”? They’ll compare.
[04:11] Markus Klein: Yeah. We position Redwood as the serving layer: you can bring open models, we can host, dedicate, or deploy private. If they’re on Bedrock, the conversation is usually “do you want more knobs and observability and predictable economics?” We don’t go hard on “Bedrock bad.”
[04:28] Soojin Lee: And for OpenAI comparisons, we focus on deployment flexibility and production tooling: routing, fallbacks, model pinning, dashboards, and cost levers.

[04:41] Elena Petrova: Okay but what can we safely claim live? Like “X ms latency.”
[04:46] Soojin Lee: Great question. We don’t commit to an absolute number in the partner deck. We can say “we target sub-second time-to-first-token for this class of model,” but even that is phrased as “in typical conditions.” In the demo we show *our* dashboard. The dashboard is the proof.
[05:05] Markus Klein: And if the dashboard is green, you show it. If it’s not, you switch to the screenshot slide and narrate.
[05:12] Rafael Mendes: We call that Plan B. Like don’t fight the environment.

[05:17] Tom Becker: Do you have like a single “if it breaks” checklist?
[05:20] Rafael Mendes: Yes. Pre-demo: verify model pinned, run smoke script, check latency panel, check 5xx panel, check throttles. Post-demo: rotate key if needed, reset quotas, clear seed data. I’ll send the one-pager.

[05:38] Soojin Lee: On the deck, there are three persona branches. Platform eng: emphasize reliability, routing, and standardization across teams. ML eng: emphasize throughput, batching/caching, quality monitoring. Security: emphasize isolation, logging, retention, residency.
[05:56] Elena Petrova: Can you say what you say on retention? This comes up constantly.
[06:01] Markus Klein: Yeah. In the demo tenant: no customer data. Logs are sanitized. In general product terms: we have configurable retention options depending on deployment mode, and for Private deployments logging can be customer-controlled. We don’t train on customer prompts. That line is important.
[06:21] Soojin Lee: We have a security FAQ doc that spells it out. We should stick to that wording.
[06:26] James Wu: And audit logs? Is it like SIEM integration?
[06:29] Rafael Mendes: We have audit logs in the platform for control-plane actions. For SIEM, we have patterns—export via webhook or forwarder. But we shouldn’t improvise specifics. If asked, we say, “We support audit logging and can integrate with common SIEMs; we’ll confirm the connector based on your stack.”
[06:50] James Wu: Okay, fair.

[06:52] Amina Hassan: EU residency question. If the customer says “must stay in EU,” what do we do?
[06:58] Markus Klein: For the standard tenant, it’s multi-region but not guaranteed EU-only for every route. For that call, we either (a) run the demo with the EU region route if it’s available, or (b) use the Private deployment narrative and explain region pinning is supported in production, then follow up with a region-specific trial.
[07:17] Soojin Lee: We have a slide that says “regional routing policies” and we keep it at capability level. We don’t show a live EU-only toggle unless we’ve verified that route.
[07:27] Elena Petrova: So: don’t demo what you can’t guarantee that day.
[07:30] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[07:33] Soojin Lee: Now, joint-call mechanics. What works best: partner opens with context and why you’re bringing Redwood in. Redwood does a 2-minute discovery: current model endpoints, volumes, latency needs, where they deploy. Then Redwood drives the API call + Console click path. Partner jumps in for procurement/commercial process questions.
[07:56] Tom Becker: Who handles pricing?
[07:58] Markus Klein: Usually Redwood AE, but if partner wants to talk packaging at a high level, that’s fine. We do not show hard numbers in the standard deck. We can talk in ranges and “drivers.”
[08:11] Amina Hassan: Yeah, our teams prefer to keep numbers out.

[08:14] Renee Sullivan: Also, we have a “2-minute mini demo” variant. It’s basically: one streaming request + show the latency panel and stop. It’s for execs or when you only have the last five minutes of a call.
[08:29] James Wu: Can we get that script? Like literally the command.
[08:33] Renee Sullivan: Yep, I’ll send. It’s one curl plus one Console page.

[08:38] Markus Klein: Okay, I’m going to share a bit about the demo scenarios so you know what’s safe for partners to run.
[08:45] Markus Klein: Scenario 1: Streaming chat. It’s our “fast path.” It demonstrates time-to-first-token and stable streaming.
[08:54] Markus Klein: Scenario 2: Tool calling / function calling. We do a simple “extract fields -> call a fake function” example. It’s not a giant integration.
[09:05] Markus Klein: Scenario 3: Fallback routing. We intentionally trigger an error on a route (or simulate a constraint) and show fallback to a compatible model.
[09:16] Markus Klein: Scenario 4: Observability. Show token-level cost, route breakdown, errors panel.

[09:24] Elena Petrova: When you say intentionally trigger an error… is that safe? Feels risky live.
[09:29] Rafael Mendes: We do it in a controlled way. But if it feels risky, we don’t do the “trigger” live. We show the routing policy and describe the behavior, then show historical data in the dashboard. Plan B.
[09:43] Soojin Lee: The talk track literally says, “We can force a failure, or we can just show you the policy and a real incident replay.”

[09:54] James Wu: On the Console, what are the click paths we should memorize?
[09:58] Renee Sullivan: Honestly, don’t memorize. Use the checklist. But the main ones:
- Routes -> select “standard-demo-chat”
- Observability -> Latency & Cost
- Rollouts -> (view) model pinning / version
- Errors -> 5xx and throttles.
[10:19] Markus Klein: And again, partners usually do not click around in Console live unless we’ve practiced.

[10:25] (crosstalk)
[10:25] Elena Petrova: So can we access Console at all?
[10:27] Markus Klein: View-only, yes.
[10:28] Rafael Mendes: Yep.

[10:31] Soojin Lee: I want to hit security Q&A because partner calls often get derailed there.
[10:37] Soojin Lee: Common questions:
- “Do you train on our data?” -> No.
- “How long do you retain prompts/logs?” -> Configurable; demo tenant uses sanitized logs; Private can be customer-controlled.
- “SSO/SAML?” -> Yes for enterprise; RBAC.
- “Encryption?” -> In transit and at rest; KMS integration depending on deployment.
- “Audit logs?” -> Yes for control-plane actions.

[11:03] Amina Hassan: And SOC2?
[11:05] Markus Klein: We have SOC 2 Type II, but we share the letter under NDA via security package. For the demo, we just state “SOC 2 Type II available.”
[11:15] Tom Becker: Great.

[11:17] Rafael Mendes: Another big one: “Where does data go?” If they’re EU, we don’t claim EU-only in the standard tenant unless we’ve verified. For Private we can do VPC and region pinning.

[11:30] James Wu: What about on-prem? We have a customer that asks on-prem first sentence.
[11:35] Markus Klein: We have an on-prem option as part of Private for regulated/air-gapped. But we don’t demo on-prem live; we talk architecture and then scope a POC. The standard demo is about the runtime and controls.

[11:49] Soojin Lee: Also we should not get dragged into kernel-level debates live. If it becomes a deep dive, schedule a technical follow-up.
[11:57] James Wu: (laughs) Yeah, fair.

[12:00] Markus Klein: Okay, let’s talk about the “joint call run.”
[12:04] Markus Klein: Roles:
- Partner AE: sets context, relationship, commercial process.
- Partner SE: discovery + validates environment.
- Redwood SE (us): drives demo tenant + console.
- Redwood AE (not on this call) typically handles pricing/packaging.
[12:22] Markus Klein: Before call: we do a 10-minute pre-brief. Confirm persona, pick scenario order, confirm whether we can run the “failure/fallback” live or we’ll do policy-only.

[12:37] Elena Petrova: Is there a rule like “always do Hosted first”?
[12:40] Soojin Lee: Default yes, because it’s fast. But if the first stakeholder is security, you can start with Private narrative and show observability + audit logs early.
[12:52] Renee Sullivan: We’ve also had success starting with “Here’s how to keep your app up if a model has a bad day.” Reliability resonates.

[13:05] James Wu: How do you handle a customer that asks “what happens when the model changes output”? Like quality drift.
[13:11] Markus Klein: We say: pin versions for stability, canary rollouts, evals / regression checks. In demo tenant we pin versions so the talk track stays consistent.
[13:23] Soojin Lee: And we can show the “rollout policy” screen view-only. That’s usually enough.

[13:31] Rafael Mendes: Slight correction: in Console it’s under “Deployments” not “Rollouts” for some accounts, depending on UI flag.
[13:38] Soojin Lee: Yes, thank you. We’ll annotate that in partner notes because that UI label has changed once.

[13:47] Tom Becker: That’s a good point. UI drift is a killer for partners.
[13:50] Renee Sullivan: Yep. That’s why we’ve got screenshots in the deck as fallback.

[14:00] Markus Klein: Let’s do escalation path. Rafael?
[14:03] Rafael Mendes: Sure. If the tenant is slow or errors:
1) Don’t debug live. Switch to screenshot slide and narrate.
2) If you have time, run the smoke script again; sometimes it’s a transient.
3) Ping #demo-tenant-ops (Slack) with: timestamp, route name, region, request id if you have it.
4) Business hours paging goes to oncall rotation. If it’s outside, we’ll respond best-effort, but for partner calls we try to keep calls inside supported windows.
[14:34] Elena Petrova: So for partner calls, we should schedule in those windows.
[14:37] Rafael Mendes: Ideally, yes.

[14:41] Amina Hassan: What about throttles? We had a trial last quarter where we hit 429s in the middle.
[14:46] Markus Klein: Demo tenant quotas are set to avoid that. But if you do something weird like run a load test, you can still hit it. The scripts are tuned to stay under the limits.
[14:58] Renee Sullivan: And we tell folks: don’t refresh the “run request” button ten times.
[15:02] (laughter)

[15:06] Soojin Lee: Before we wrap, I want to call out messaging constraints. Partners should not say:
- “We guarantee X latency”
- “This will always be cheaper than OpenAI”
- “EU-only residency today” unless confirmed
Instead say:
- “Here are the levers and observed metrics in this environment”
- “We can deploy hosted/dedicated/private depending on requirements”
- “We’ll validate in a POC with your workload”

[15:37] James Wu: Makes sense.

[15:39] Elena Petrova: Can you send us the security FAQ and the wording? We’ve had deals blow up on one sloppy sentence.
[15:46] Markus Klein: Yes. Soojin will send deck + notes, Renee will send scripts, Rafael sends escalation/checklist.

[15:56] Tom Becker: Any requirements on our side to get access? SSO, domain verification?
[16:01] Renee Sullivan: We’ll need a list of emails, and we’ll map them to RBAC. If your folks don’t have SSO set up, we can do a short-lived key, but we prefer SSO.
[16:14] Elena Petrova: Okay, I’ll send the list.

[16:17] Markus Klein: Great. We also recommend one dry run where you play “security persona” and we timebox it. We’ve found partners do better when they know what to cut.
[16:29] Amina Hassan: +1.

[16:31] Soojin Lee: One more: when you’re on a joint call, avoid jumping between Hosted, Dedicated, Private too much. It confuses buyers. Pick a path.
[16:42] James Wu: So basically: ask one or two questions and then commit.
[16:45] Soojin Lee: Exactly.

[16:48] Markus Klein: Okay, we’re at time. Any last questions?
[16:53] Elena Petrova: None. This was super helpful.
[16:55] James Wu: Same.
[16:56] Tom Becker: All good.

[16:58] Markus Klein: Cool. We’ll send the assets today and tomorrow. Thanks all.

(End of transcript)

NOTES
- Several UI labels referenced (Rollouts vs Deployments) may differ by account; use screenshots as backup.
- Partner access should remain view-only for routes/policies; Redwood to drive Console changes live.
